column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 46: “Every intoxicant is unlawful”

column2: From Abū Burdah, from his father, Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī: The Prophet ﷺ sent him to Yemen, and he asked him about drinks that were made there. He said: “And what are they?”
He said: Bitʿ and mizr. Abū Burdah was asked: What is bitʿ?
He said: Nabīdh [a steeped drink] of honey; and mizr is nabīdh of barley. He said: “Every intoxicant is unlawful.” Al-Bukhārī recorded it.

Muslim recorded it too, and his wording is: He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent me and Muʿādh to Yemen, and I said: Messenger of Allah, a drink is made in our land called mizr, from barley, and a drink called bitʿ, from honey. He said: “Every intoxicant is unlawful.”

In a narration of Muslim's he said: “Everything that intoxicates one away from the prayer is unlawful.” In another narration of his, he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had been given comprehensive words and their conclusions, so he said: “I forbid every intoxicant that intoxicates one away from the prayer.”

This hadith is a foundation for the prohibition of consuming any intoxicant, anything that covers the mind. Allah has mentioned in His Book the cause that makes intoxicants prohibited. Wine (khamr) was first prohibited at the times of prayer, after one of the Emigrants prayed,

recited in his prayer and muddled his recitation; and the words of the Exalted were revealed: “O you who believe, do not approach the prayer while you are intoxicated, until you know what you are saying” [al-Nisāʾ 4:43].
After that the caller of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to call out: No one who is intoxicated is to approach the prayer. Then Allah prohibited it absolutely, with His words, Exalted is He:

“Wine, gambling, idolatrous altars and divining arrows are only a filth of Satan's handiwork, so avoid it, that you may prosper. Satan only wants to cast enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling, and to turn you away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer. So will you not desist?” [al-Māʾidah 5:90–91].

Here He, Glorified is He, mentioned the reason why wine and maysir — that is, gambling — are prohibited: through them Satan casts enmity and hatred among people. Whoever is intoxicated, his reason is disordered,

and he may set about harming people in their persons and their property, and may even go as far as killing. It is the mother of vile things: whoever drinks it may kill and fornicate, and may even disbelieve.
This meaning has been narrated from ʿUthmān and others, and it has also been narrated as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ).
As for the gambler, he may be beaten and have his wealth taken from him against his will until nothing is left to him, and then his rancour against the one who took his wealth grows intense.

Whatever leads to enmity and hatred is unlawful. He, Glorified is He, also told us that Satan turns people away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer through wine and gambling. The intoxicated person's mind is lost or disordered, so he cannot remember Allah

or pray. That is why a group of the Salaf said: The wine-drinker passes through an hour in which he does not know his Lord. Allah, Glorified is He, created His creatures only so that they would know Him, remember Him, worship Him and obey Him; so whatever leads to abstaining from that,

and stands between the servant and knowing his Lord, remembering Him and conversing with Him, is prohibited — and that is intoxication. Sleep is different. Allah the Exalted made His servants by nature to need it and compelled them to it, and their bodies cannot be sustained without it, since it gives them rest from striving and toil;

so it is among the greatest of Allah's blessings to His servants. When the believer sleeps as much as he needs and then wakes to remember Allah, converse with Him and call on Him, his sleep helps him to pray and to remember. That is why one of the Companions said: I hope for reward for my sleep just as I hope for reward for my standing [in prayer].

Gambling likewise turns people away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer. The gambler's heart stays devoted to it, and it distracts him from all his interests and concerns, so that he barely remembers them, being so absorbed in it.
That is why ʿAlī, when he passed some people playing chess, said: “What are these images to which you are devoted?” [al-Anbiyāʾ 21:52].
He likened them to those who were devoted to images.
A hadith says: “The one addicted to wine is like a worshipper of an idol.” His heart becomes attached to it, so that he can hardly leave it, just as the idol-worshipper does not leave his worship.

All of this is opposed to what Allah created His servants for: emptying their hearts for knowing Him, loving Him, fearing Him, remembering Him, conversing with Him, calling on Him and humbly beseeching Him. Whatever stands between the servant and that,

when the servant has no necessity for it and it is, rather, pure harm to him, is prohibited. It has been narrated that ʿAlī said to some people he saw playing chess: This is not what you were created for.
From this it is known that maysir is unlawful, whether it is played for a stake or without one, and that chess is like backgammon or worse,
because it distracts those who play it from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer more than backgammon does.
The point is that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Every intoxicant is unlawful,” and “Everything that intoxicates one away from the prayer is unlawful.”

The hadiths from the Prophet ﷺ to this effect are mass-transmitted (mutawātir). Both al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Ibn ʿUmar, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Every intoxicant is wine, and all wine is unlawful.” Muslim's wording is: “and every intoxicant is unlawful.”

Both also recorded, from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah, that the Prophet ﷺ was asked about bitʿ and said: “Every drink that intoxicates is unlawful.” In a narration of Muslim's: “Every intoxicating drink is unlawful.” Aḥmad and Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn declared this hadith authentic

and used it as evidence. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr reported that the people of knowledge of hadith are agreed that it is authentic, and that it is the most firmly established report from the Prophet ﷺ on the prohibition of intoxicants.
As for the criticism of it that some Ḥanafī jurists have reported from Ibn Maʿīn, it is not established from him.
Muslim also recorded, from the hadith of Abū al-Zubayr, from Jābir, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Every intoxicant is unlawful.”

This is the view of the great majority of Muslim scholars, among the Companions, the Successors and the scholars of the great cities after them. It is the position of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, al-Layth, al-Awzāʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan and others, and it is one of the views on which the people of Madīnah were all agreed.
Various groups of the scholars of al-Kūfah disagreed, saying: Wine (khamr) is grape wine alone; of anything else, only the amount that intoxicates is unlawful,

and less than that is not. The scholars of the great cities never ceased to reject this from them, even though they held it by independent reasoning (ijtihād) and are forgiven for it, and among them were many leading figures in knowledge and religion.
Ibn al-Mubārak said: I have not found an authentic concession regarding nabīdh from anyone except Ibrāhīm — meaning al-Nakhaʿī. Imam Aḥmad likewise denied that anything authentic exists on it.
He compiled the book al-Ashribah (“Drinks”) and mentioned no concession in it; and he compiled a book on wiping over leather socks
and mentioned in it that some of the Salaf rejected wiping. He was asked: How is it that you did not put the concession in al-Ashribah, as you put [the dissenting view] in the book on wiping?
He said: There is no authentic hadith granting a concession for intoxicants.

Among what shows that every intoxicant is wine is that the prohibition of wine was revealed in Madīnah because its people asked about the drinks they had, and there was no grape wine there. Had the verse prohibiting wine not covered what they had,

it would have explained nothing of what they had asked about, and the very occasion of its revelation would have fallen outside the general scope of its words, which is impossible. When the prohibition of wine was revealed, they poured out the drinks they had, which shows that they understood these to be part of the wine they had been commanded to avoid.
In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from Anas, who said: Wine was prohibited to us when it was prohibited, and we found little grape wine; most of our wine was from unripe dates (busr) and dried dates.

He also said: I was serving drink to Abū Ṭalḥah, Abū Dujānah and Suhayl ibn Bayḍāʾ — a mixture of unripe and dried dates — when wine was prohibited, and I threw it out. I was their cupbearer and the youngest of them, and at that time we counted it as wine.
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, also from him, he said: We had no wine other than this faḍīkh of yours [a drink of crushed unripe dates], the one you call faḍīkh.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from him, he said: Allah sent down the verse in which He prohibited wine at a time when the only drink drunk in Madīnah was made from dates.
In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: The prohibition of wine was revealed when there were five drinks in Madīnah at the time, and none of them was a drink of grapes.

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from al-Shaʿbī, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: ʿUmar stood on the pulpit and said: To proceed: the prohibition of wine has been revealed, and it is made from five things: grapes, dates, honey, wheat and barley.
Wine (khamr) is whatever befogs (khāmara) the mind.
Imam Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī recorded it from the hadith of al-Shaʿbī, from al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, from the Prophet ﷺ.
Al-Tirmidhī mentioned that the version of those who said “from al-Shaʿbī, from Ibn ʿUmar, from ʿUmar” is more correct, and Ibn al-Madīnī said the same.
Abū Isḥāq narrated from Abū Burdah, who said: ʿUmar said: Whatever you have fermented and aged is wine; and where would we have had grape wine?
In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, from al-Mukhtār ibn Fulful, who said: I asked Anas ibn Mālik about drinking from [different kinds of] vessels, and he said:
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade pitch-lined vessels, and he said: “Every intoxicant is unlawful.” I said to him: You are right, intoxication is unlawful; but what about a drink or two with our meal?

He said: Of an intoxicant, a little and a lot are both unlawful. He also said: Wine is from grapes, dates, honey, wheat, barley and sorghum; whatever of these you have fermented is wine. Aḥmad recorded it from ʿAbdullāh ibn Idrīs: I heard al-Mukhtār ibn Fulful say… and he mentioned it. This chain meets Muslim's conditions.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Wine is from these two trees: the date palm and the vine.” This states explicitly that date nabīdh is wine.

A small amount of whatever intoxicates in large amounts has also been forbidden explicitly, as in the hadith of Jābir that Abū Dāwūd, Ibn Mājah and al-Tirmidhī recorded, al-Tirmidhī grading it good, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whatever intoxicates in large amounts, a small amount of it is unlawful.”

Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī, who graded it good, recorded from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Every intoxicant is unlawful, and whatever a faraq [a large measure] of it intoxicates, a palmful of it is unlawful.” In one narration: “a sip of it is unlawful.” Aḥmad used it as evidence and held this view.
He was asked about someone who said that it is not authentic.
He said: This man is mughlī — meaning that he has gone to extremes in what he says.

Al-Nasāʾī recorded this hadith in the narrations of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ and ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, from the Prophet ﷺ, and it has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ by many routes that would take too long to mention.
Ibn ʿAjlān narrated from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb: Abū Wahb al-Jayshānī told me, from the delegation of the people of Yemen, that they came to the Prophet ﷺ
and asked him about drinks found in Yemen. He said: They named for him bitʿ, from honey, and mizr, from barley. The Prophet ﷺ said: “Do you become intoxicated from them?”
They said: If we drink a lot, we become intoxicated. He said: “Then a little of whatever intoxicates in large amounts is unlawful.” The judge Ismāʿīl recorded it.

The Companions used to cite the Prophet's words ﷺ, “Every intoxicant is unlawful,” as evidence that every kind of intoxicant is prohibited, both those that existed in the time of the Prophet ﷺ and those that appeared after him.

So when Ibn ʿAbbās was asked about bādhaq [a cooked grape drink], he said: Muḥammad came before bādhaq; whatever intoxicates is unlawful. Al-Bukhārī recorded it. He meant that if it intoxicates, it falls under this comprehensive, general statement.
Know that intoxicants that remove the mind are of two kinds.
The first is whatever brings pleasure and exhilaration. This is the wine whose drinking is prohibited. In the Musnad, from Ṭalq al-Ḥanafī: He was sitting with the Prophet ﷺ
when a man said to him: Messenger of Allah, what do you think of a drink we make in our land from our fruits?
He ﷺ said: “Who is it that asks about the intoxicant?

Do not drink it, and do not give it to your Muslim brother to drink. By the One in whose hand is my soul” — or: by that by which one swears — “no man drinks it seeking the pleasure of its intoxication but Allah will give him wine to drink on the Day of Resurrection.”

A group of scholars said: It makes no difference whether this intoxicant is solid or liquid, eaten or drunk, or made from grain, fruit, milk or anything else. They included in it hashish, which is made from the leaves of hemp,
and other things that are eaten for their pleasure and intoxication. In the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd, from the hadith of Shahr ibn Ḥawshab, from Umm Salamah, who said:
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade every intoxicant and every mufattir. The mufattir is what numbs the body, even if it does not reach the point of intoxication.

The second is what removes the mind and intoxicates without any pleasure or exhilaration, such as banj [henbane] and the like. The scholars of our [Ḥanbalī] school said: If one takes it because one needs it as a medicine, and it is usually safe, it is permitted. It is narrated of ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr that when gangrene set into his leg

and they wanted to amputate it, the physicians said to him: We will give you a medicine to drink so that your mind goes absent and you do not feel the pain of the cutting. He refused, and said: I never thought that any creature would drink a drink that takes his mind away until he does not know his Lord.
It is also narrated that he said: I will not drink anything that comes between me and the remembrance of my Lord, the Mighty and Majestic.
If one takes it without needing it as a medicine, most of the scholars of our school, such as al-Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā, Ibn ʿAqīl and the author of al-Mughnī, said that it is prohibited,

because it is a means of removing the mind without need, and so it is prohibited, like drinking an intoxicant. Ḥanash al-Raḥabī — who has weakness — narrated from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās as marfūʿ: “Whoever drinks a drink that takes away his mind has come to one of the doors of the major sins.”
A group of them, among them Ibn ʿAqīl in his Funūn, said that it is not unlawful,
because there is no pleasure in it. Wine was prohibited only because of the exhilarating potency in it, and there is neither exhilaration nor potency in banj and the like.

On the view of the majority, then, if someone takes it without need, becomes intoxicated by it and pronounces a divorce, his divorce is judged as the divorce of a drunk. Most of the scholars of our school, such as Ibn Ḥāmid and al-Qāḍī, said this,
and so did al-Shāfiʿī's followers. The Ḥanafīs said that his divorce does not take effect, giving as their reason that there is no pleasure in it; this shows that they did not hold it prohibited.

The Shāfiʿīs said: It is prohibited, and there are two views on whether divorce takes effect under it. The apparent sense of Aḥmad's words is that his divorce does not take effect, unlike the drunk's. Al-Qāḍī interpreted this, saying: He said it only to hold the Ḥanafīs to their own principle, not as his own belief. The context of his words allows for that.
As for the prescribed punishment (ḥadd), it is due only for consuming intoxicants that have potency and exhilaration,
because these are what people's souls are drawn to, and so the ḥadd was made a deterrent from them.
What intoxicates without exhilaration or pleasure carries no more than a discretionary punishment (taʿzīr),
because nothing in people's souls draws them to it, such that a fixed punishment would be needed to deter them. It is like eating carrion and pork, or drinking blood.

Most of the scholars who hold that a small amount of whatever intoxicates in large amounts is prohibited also hold that the ḥadd is applied to someone who drinks what intoxicates in large amounts, even if he believes it lawful on the basis of an interpretation. This is the view of al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad, unlike Abū Thawr, who said: He is not given the ḥadd, because of his interpretation; he is like someone who marries without a guardian.
There is also disagreement over the ḥadd for one who marries without a guardian, but the correct view is that he is not given the ḥadd.

Some have distinguished between him and the one who drinks nabīdh on the basis of an interpretation: drinking the disputed nabīdh invites one to drink the wine whose prohibition is agreed upon, whereas marrying without a guardian frees one from any need for fornication, whose prohibition is agreed upon, and leads one to keep chaste from it.
What Aḥmad stated explicitly is that he applied the ḥadd to one who drinks nabīdh on the basis of an interpretation only
because his interpretation is weak and does not avert the ḥadd from him. For he said, in the narration of al-Athram: Whoever drinks nabīdh on the basis of an interpretation is given the ḥadd;

yet if someone is brought before the ruler who pronounced an irrevocable divorce (al-battah) and then took his wife back, interpreting the irrevocable divorce as a single one, while the ruler holds that it is three, the couple are not separated.
He said: This is not like that. The matter [of wine] is clear in the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Prophet ﷺ. The prohibition of wine was revealed when their drink was faḍīkh,
and the Prophet ﷺ said: “Every intoxicant is wine.” This is clear, whereas the irrevocable divorce is a matter on which people have disagreed.
